quizzes.title: Checkpoint 1 — Capture, Priorities, and Planning
quizzes.intro: Check foundations before focus, habits, and boundaries.

questions.prompt: Why do systems beat motivation alone?

options.text: Because motivation is always permanent
Because systems provide defaults on ordinary days when mood is uneven
Because systems remove the need for any priorities
Because apps automatically know what matters

questions.explanation: Motivation is weather; systems are climate—repeatable rules that work on normal days.

wrongExplanations.d: Apps store priorities; they do not create them.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a project and a next action?

options.text: They are the same thing
A project needs multiple steps; a next action is a concrete doable step
A next action is always a multi-month outcome
Projects should never be broken down

questions.explanation: Lists fail when fuzzy projects sit where actions should be.

wrongExplanations.a: The lesson separates them on purpose.
wrongExplanations.c: That describes a project, not a next action.
wrongExplanations.d: Breakdown is how stuck projects move.

questions.prompt: What does important versus urgent thinking emphasize?

options.text: That every notification is equally strategic
Protecting work aligned with goals, not only time pressure
Ignoring all deadlines forever
Letting other people’s emergencies always win by default

questions.explanation: Important work needs protection; urgency alone is a poor compass.

wrongExplanations.c: Deadlines still matter; prioritization is not avoidance.
wrongExplanations.d: Defaulting to others’ urgency is a failure mode.

questions.prompt: What belongs in a weekly planning ritual?

options.text: Clear inboxes, update projects, choose a few priorities, and place deep-work blocks
Schedule forty equal priorities with no slack
Skip the calendar entirely
Switch productivity apps every weekend

questions.explanation: A short weekly review resets commitments and protects what matters.

questions.prompt: What is a common daily planning mistake?

options.text: Choosing a realistic top three based on true free time
Planning six hours of deep work on a day with four hours of meetings
Leaving a little slack for interruptions
Checking capture inboxes on a schedule

questions.explanation: Fantasy planning ignores calendar truth and creates failure spirals.

wrongExplanations.d: Scheduled processing supports a trusted system.

quizzes.title: Checkpoint 2 — Focus, Energy, and Boundaries
quizzes.intro: Test focus design, habits, energy, and saying no.

questions.prompt: When focus fails, what should you do first according to the lesson?

options.text: Only shame yourself harder
Diagnose whether the blocker is unclear next steps, fear, boredom, exhaustion, or interruption
Buy a new app immediately
Add twelve more tasks

questions.explanation: Different diagnoses need different fixes; shame is not a schedule.

questions.prompt: What is energy management in this course?

options.text: Treating all hours as identical
Placing demanding work in higher-energy windows when possible
Ignoring sleep as irrelevant
Only counting steps on a tracker

questions.explanation: Hours differ in quality; match task difficulty to energy when you can.

wrongExplanations.d: Trackers alone are not the point.

options.text: With an elaborate routine that needs a free weekend
Tiny and stacked onto existing anchors
By changing every habit on day one
Only after buying premium stationery

questions.explanation: Tiny anchored habits survive; oversized launches fail.

wrongExplanations.d: Tools are optional; consistency is not.

questions.prompt: What is true about saying no?

options.text: Time management without boundaries is incomplete
Every yes has unlimited capacity behind it
You should never renegotiate scope
Calendars cannot fill with overcommitment

questions.explanation: Boundaries and renegotiation protect priorities and quality.

wrongExplanations.c: Scope negotiation is a core skill.
wrongExplanations.d: Overcommitment shows up as burnout or quiet failure.

questions.prompt: What is a healthy minimal tool stack?

options.text: Seventeen apps with the same tasks duplicated
Calendar for time, tasks for actions/projects, notes for reference
Only memory and vibes
A new system every Monday

questions.explanation: Separation of calendar, tasks, and notes keeps the system trustworthy.

quizzes.title: Final Quiz — Sustainability, Collaboration, and Judgment
quizzes.intro: Use the full lesson. Focus on recovery, metrics, collaboration, and durable practice.

questions.prompt: How should meetings be treated in a time system?

options.text: As free and endless by default
As expensive; ask for outcomes and decline message-worthy meetings when possible
As replacements for all deep work
As events that never need actions or owners

questions.explanation: Meeting discipline protects maker time and follow-through.

questions.prompt: What helps with procrastination according to the lesson?

options.text: Only harsher self-criticism
Smaller steps, timers, lower first-draft bars, and curiosity about the blocker
Adding vague mega-tasks to the list
Deleting the project silently and hoping

questions.explanation: Procrastination often hides emotion; practical unblocking beats shame.

wrongExplanations.d: Silent abandonment is not a system.

questions.prompt: Which metrics help evaluate a time system?

options.text: Only how stressed you look
Priority outcomes completed, protected deep-work hours, review consistency, and stress trends
Number of apps installed
How colorful the planner is

questions.explanation: Outcome and sustainability metrics beat vanity productivity theater.

wrongExplanations.c: App count is a vanity metric.

questions.prompt: What should a shutdown ritual include?

options.text: Leaving every loop unnamed for mystery
Capturing loose ends, setting tomorrow’s top priorities, and closing the day deliberately
Starting five new projects at 11pm
Checking every notification one last frantic time with no capture

questions.explanation: Shutdowns close loops and prepare future you.

questions.prompt: How should managers and makers think about schedules?

options.text: Everyone thrives on identical fragmented days
Maker work needs longer blocks; management often fragments—label days or half-days when you are both
Makers never need communication windows
Context collapse is the ideal forever state

questions.explanation: Mode clustering reduces switching costs when roles collide.

wrongExplanations.c: Communication still matters; it can be batched.
wrongExplanations.d: Always-available and always-creating burns people out.

questions.prompt: Which standard captures the course’s end goal?

options.text: Manage time so your days reflect your priorities in writing—not only in wishes
Collect systems forever without using one
Fill every minute until burnout proves commitment
Let urgency and inbox noise set every agenda

questions.explanation: Alignment between priorities and lived schedule is the real product of the system.

wrongExplanations.b: Tool collecting is a listed mistake.
wrongExplanations.d: Default inbox agendas fight intentional work.
